chapters.title: Prefixes and Suffixes
chapters.snippet: Adding 'un-' or '-less' to a word can flip its whole meaning — like turning 'happy' into 'unhappy'!

The prefix 'bi-' means...

The suffix '-ful' means...
The suffix '-less' means...

chapters.title: Reading Comprehension
chapters.snippet: From Jane Goodall's chimpanzees to a mysterious house called Cogston, great readers notice every clue in a story!

questions.title: Jane Goodall
questions.body:
Jane Goodall was born on 3rd April 1934 in London, England, to her parents Margaret Joseph and Mortimer Morris-Goodall. As a little girl, her father once gave her a stuffed toy chimpanzee named Jubilee instead of a teddy bear — and Jane still has it today, even though she's all grown up!

That gift sparked a lifelong love of animals. In 1957, Jane travelled to Kenya, where she met a scientist named Louis Leakey. He taught her all about chimpanzees, and Jane went on to live alongside them in the wild for over 55 years.

Unlike other scientists, who only gave the chimps numbers, Jane gave each one a name — like David Greybeard, named for his grey chin. Naming them helped her notice that every chimpanzee had its own personality: some were loud, some quiet, some kind, and some grumpy, just like people!

Jane made several surprising discoveries. She once watched a chimpanzee poke a blade of grass into a termite mound and lick off the insects — the very first time anyone had seen an animal use a tool. She also learned that chimpanzees eat meat as well as plants, and that they show real feelings like happiness, sadness, and anger.

Remember: chimpanzees are apes, not monkeys — gorillas and orangutans are apes too! In 2002, Jane was honoured with an award for her decades spent helping animals and wildlife around the world.

questions.title: The Curse of Cogston House
questions.body:
Jack and Luca, both eleven years old, usually spent their evenings on the swings at the park. But today, Jack had a different idea. “Come on, this is going to be epic!” he said, pushing through the overgrown bushes toward a part of the park everyone called ‘The Top End’.

Luca followed more slowly. He wasn't sure he wanted to leave the swings behind, and he liked The Top End even less — but he didn't want to be left behind either, so he pushed on through the nettles and brambles after his friend.

Eventually the two boys reached a clearing, and there it was: Cogston House, wrapped from top to bottom in rusty scaffolding that looked like it was the only thing holding the crumbling walls together. Nearly a hundred years old, the house had once belonged to a wealthy family, but nobody had lived there for about thirty years. Ivy crept over the broken bricks, and the whole place felt heavy with sadness.

Everybody in town seemed to have their own story about Cogston House — some said it was cursed, some said it was haunted — but no one really knew which parts were true and which were just rumours. Luca, for one, wasn't keen to stick around and find out.

questions.title: Three Aesop's Fables
questions.body:
The Crow and the Pitcher
During a dry spell, a thirsty crow found a pitcher with a little water in it. But the pitcher was tall with a narrow neck, and no matter how hard he tried, the crow couldn't reach the water. Then he had a clever idea: he began dropping small pebbles into the pitcher, one by one. Each pebble made the water rise a little higher, until at last it was high enough for the crow to drink.

The Fox and the Stork
A fox once decided to play a trick on his neighbor, the stork. “Come and dine with me today,” he said, smiling to himself. When the stork arrived, hungry and looking forward to a good meal, the fox served soup in a wide, shallow dish. The fox lapped it up easily, but the stork could only wet the tip of his long bill — not a single drop passed his lips. Rather than getting angry, the calm stork invited the fox to dine with him in return. This time, the meal was served in a tall jar with a narrow neck. The stork ate happily with his long bill, while the fox could only sniff at the delicious smell from outside the jar. “Don't play tricks on your neighbors,” the stork said calmly, “unless you can take the same trick yourself.”

The Bear and the Bees
While wandering through the woods hunting for berries, a bear stumbled upon a fallen log full of honey, buzzing with a swarm of bees. He sniffed carefully around the log, wondering if the bees were home. Just then, a bee returning from the fields spotted him, guessed exactly what he was after, and stung him sharply before disappearing back into the log. Furious, the bear lost his temper at once — he clawed at the log to destroy the whole nest. But that only brought the entire swarm out after him, and the poor bear had to run for his life, finally escaping by diving straight into a pool of water.
